The map moved this week. Russia and Ukraine hit each other's capitals. The Strait of Hormuz became a bargaining chip. Darfur fell. The Durand Line lit up. And migrants fled South Africa.

5 ways the lines shifted this week — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Russia launched one of its biggest strikes on Kyiv in weeks — 8-10 killed, children among them, buildings ablaze — hours after Zelensky warned of a "massive" attack.

Days earlier Ukraine downed 419 drones over Russia. Both capitals are now targets.
(BBC, Guardian, AJ, NYT)

2/ After a short US–Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz — ~1/5 of world oil — is the bargaining chip.

Talks in Doha, fresh strikes on Bahrain & Kuwait, and Iran now rejecting the 1968 pact on the strait's shipping lanes.

Control of a few miles reshapes the Gulf. (Guardian, NYT)

3/ Amnesty says Sudan's RSF committed crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing taking el-Fasher, Darfur's last army-held city. The UN cites "hallmarks of genocide."

It hardens a de facto split of Sudan: RSF west, army east.
(BBC, Guardian, DW)

4/ Pakistan and the Taliban traded fire across the Durand Line. Afghan officials say Pakistani airstrikes killed 36 civilians; Pakistan says it downed Taliban drones.

The 1893 colonial border Kabul never recognized is a live front again.
(BBC, Guardian)

5/ 2,000+ anti-foreigner protesters marched in Durban as a deadline passed for undocumented migrants to leave. Police deployed, fearing a repeat of 2008's deadly xenophobic violence.

Nigeria will seek compensation for property left behind.
(Guardian, BBC)

The historical parallel 🗺️

"Who Controls Afghanistan, 2021: April vs August." In April the government (grey) held the cities. By August the map was almost all red — the Taliban swept the country in weeks.

That collapse produced the government now trading fire with Pakistan.
